narrative:
**HEADLINE**
Macro risk stands at High, anchored by structural leverage, supply-chain weaponization, and opaque credit expansion with no intraday changes.

**STORIES AT ELEVATED OR HIGHER**
No stories moved today; sustained pressures remain:
• **Private credit's opaque expansion** (High): Unregulated leverage in shadow finance creates counterparty and liquidity blindness.
• **Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade** (High): Yen carry unwind risk paired with fiscal sustainability concerns.
• **AI power & the grid bottleneck** (High): Demand surge outpacing infrastructure; brownout and capex strain.
• **Sea lanes & undersea cables** (High): Geopolitical chokepoints threaten data and energy routes.
• **Critical minerals as a weapon** (High): Supply concentration enables supply-side coercion.
• **Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)** (Elevated): Leverage embedded in financing structures obscures systemic risk.
• **Developing-world debt crisis** (Elevated): Currency and refinancing pressure on emerging sovereigns.

**WATCH**
Private credit's opaque expansion is the highest-risk story; its scale and opacity prevent market pricing of stress scenarios.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: The Fitch inclusive TTM private-credit default rate (counting distressed exchanges and LMEs) ticked up to 6.1% in July 2026 from the prior record of 6.0% set in Q2; this is applied directly as the rubric-anchored Fitch inclusive measure, with the July 2026 Fitch publication as the as_of period. One LinkedIn snippet from Fitch's own page cited '5.2% in July' but context suggests this references a sub-index (possibly PMR or count-based), not the headline inclusive TTM rate that Bloomberg and CryptoBriefing confirm at 6.1%.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings' July 2026 US Corporate Distressed and Default Monitor reported the trailing 12-month private credit default rate (inclusive of distressed exchanges and LMEs) reached approximately 6.1%, a new record high, up from 6.0% in Q2 2026. Source: Bloomberg 2026-07-30 (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-30/fitch-s-private-credit-default-rate-hit-record-in-second-quarter) and cryptobriefing.com summary of Fitch July 2026 monitor (https://cryptobriefing.com/fitch-us-corporate-default-rates-july-2026/).

dissent.view: With Intelligence estimated the 'true' private credit default rate (inclusive of selective defaults and LMEs) approached ~5% through 9M 2025, materially below the concurrent Fitch inclusive reading
Moody's noted ~65% of 2025 private credit defaults were distressed restructurings; excluding them yields headline rates of 1.6%-4.7%
Fitch LinkedIn post title references '5.2% in July' — possibly a sub-index or count-based variant, not the headline inclusive TTM rate

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: Named gating/capped funds in Q2 2026 number well above 3 and their combined AUM (BCRED ~$79B + HPS ~$26B + OCIC ~$34B alone = ~$139B) far exceeds the $100B rubric threshold, with Fitch confirming 10 of 16 tracked BDCs breaching caps in the same quarter -- a clear WIDESPREAD (2) classification.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings tracked 10 of 16 non-traded BDCs breaching their 5%-of-NAV quarterly repurchase caps in Q2 2026; Robert A. Stanger & Co. recorded repurchase requests at 12.4% of NAV (highest on record), with sponsors fulfilling only 38% and leaving ~$9.6B unfilled. Named gating funds in Q2 include: Blackstone BCRED (~$79B NAV), BlackRock HPS Corporate Lending Fund (~$26B), Blue Owl Credit Income Corp (~$34B), Blue Owl Technology Income Corp (OTIC, 38.1% request rate), Apollo Debt Solutions, and Cliffwater CCLFX. Blue Owl OBDC II ($1.6B) permanently closed redemptions in Q1 2026. Sources: Fitch Ratings via angelinvestorsnetwork.com (2026-08-20); Robert A. Stanger & Co. via tradingmarketsignals.com (2026-08-17); whitesecuritieslaw.com (July 2026); wildscrew.wordpress.com citing Bloomberg (2026-07-02).

dissent.view: Some analysts (CLA Wealth Advisors, CAIA, PGIM) argue funds are 'operating as designed' within contractual caps, not in crisis, and that request spikes reflect sentiment rather than credit deterioration -- implying the word 'gating' overstates structural stress.
Early Q3 2026 data (Golub GCRED cleared July 29 tender in full; three NAV BDCs showing 4.6% requests vs 7.9% in Q2) suggest the redemption wave may be peaking and stress is easing as of August 2026.

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: Multiple pending exemptive-relief requests (SIFMA inter-affiliate, IIB non-U.S., 15c3-3 margin), an explicit documentation/legal-agreement backlog flagged by TBAC, and industry skepticism about infrastructure readiness squarely match rubric level 1 (documentation backlog, pending exemptive relief). No deadline extension or operational failure justifies level 2, and the open relief requests and legal backlogs preclude level 0. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-08-07 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: SEC Commissioner Uyeda's August 7, 2026 statement confirms deadlines remain intact (cash 2026-12-31, repo 2027-06-30) but notes: (1) SIFMA and IIB exemptive-relief requests (inter-affiliate scope, non-U.S. transactions) are still pending SEC action after comment periods closed; (2) a new Rule 15c3-3 net-omnibus margin exemption is out for comment with a deadline of August 31, 2026; (3) documentation backlog persists — TBAC May 2026 report identifies bilateral legal agreements as 'the largest challenge from an implementation standpoint'; (4) industry expert Glenn Handley (SecFin Solutions, May 2026) wrote 'The infrastructure is not [ready].' DTCC's own FICC survey (July 2026) shows 'most' members already prepared or completing final readiness, but the fi-desk.com summary (August 2026) notes 'meaningful work remains.' No deadline extension has been granted; no operational test failure reported. Sources: SEC.gov Uyeda statement Aug 7 2026; TBAC Charge1Q2 2026 PDF (home.treasury.gov, May 2026); fi-desk.com Aug 2026; finadium.com FICC survey Jul 2026.

dissent.view: DTCC/FICC member survey (Jul 2026) reports 'most' full-service Netting Members already prepared or in final readiness activities, suggesting closer to smooth (level 0) for FICC direct participants
Industry practitioner Glenn Handley (SecFin Solutions, May 2026) argues infrastructure is not ready and deadlines are fixed but infrastructure lags, implying risk of level 2

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: Affirm 30+ DPD rose +18 bps YoY to 2.7% -- up but far short of the 100 bps spike threshold for level 2; industry charge-offs remain ~1.8-2%, below the 3% containment ceiling, squarely fitting rubric level 1 (RISING, charge-offs contained). BTIG's all-time-high ABS vintage flag is a leading indicator of further deterioration but does not yet produce a reported figure breaching the level-2 thresholds.
items.fact: Affirm FQ2'26 Shareholder Letter (filed Feb 6, 2026, period ended Dec 31, 2025): '30+ day delinquencies excluding Peloton and Pay in X loans increased 18 basis points year over year and decreased 7 basis points quarter over quarter to 2.7%.' Allowance for credit losses 5.4% of loans held for investment. Industry BNPL charge-off rate per CFPB/Richmond Fed: 1.83% in 2023, estimated ~1.8-2% in 2024-25 (well below 3%). BTIG Research (~Aug 21, 2026) separately flagged Affirm ABS 30-59 DPD at all-time highs for newest vintages.

dissent.view: BTIG Research (Aug 21, 2026) reports Affirm ABS 30-59 DPD at all-time highs for newest 2025-X2 vintage at 9 and 16 months of age, suggesting trend may be accelerating toward level 2 if it continues into H2 2026
Statista citing Affirm data through Q2 2025 showed a YoY decrease in 30+ DPD at that snapshot, suggesting the direction was briefly stable/improving before reversing

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The rubric calls for the latest published Trepp CMBS office delinquency percent; 11.76% is the most recent explicitly cited Trepp office sub-rate in public sources (Oct 2025). The July 2026 data likely exceeds this given large new office delinquencies, but no confirmed figure was retrievable, warranting medium confidence on the Oct 2025 anchor. [vintage guard: new read is 2025-10-31 data but the prior applied value was 2026-03 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate hit a new all-time high of 11.76% in October 2025, per CommercialSearch/Trepp data (https://www.commercialsearch.com/news/cmbs-delinquency-rates/). The July 2026 Trepp overall CMBS rate rose to 7.86% (+51 bps) with office towers among the largest newly delinquent loans, but no public Trepp office sub-rate for July 2026 was available in accessible summaries.

dissent.view: KBRA-rated CMBS office delinquency rate was 13.9% in January 2026 (rose 156 bps that month), a materially higher figure but reflects a different rated universe than Trepp's broader dataset
S&P Global headline for January 2026 states 'The Office Rate Surpasses 10.5%' for US CMBS, consistent with Trepp range but a separate methodology

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: CoreWeave is a named borrower explicitly facing a 2026 refinancing wall with CDS at distressed-borrower levels (855 bps/50% default odds), and AI data center debt is being offloaded at a discount in secondary markets (PIMCO/Oracle-linked paper) — both are rubric-1 triggers. No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or outright failed refinancing has been documented as of 2026-08-24, so rubric-2 is not met.
items.fact: CoreWeave's 5-year CDS spread hit ~855 bps on July 29 2026 (implying ~50% cumulative default probability); its $2.6B GPU-backed loan facility closed August 10 2026 only after spreads flexed 125 bps to clear; and the company carries a documented $4.2B refinancing wall on pre-2026 GPU-collateralized debt against sharply depreciated H100 collateral (-70-90% rental rates). PIMCO moved to sell >$14B of Oracle-linked AI data center debt in secondary markets. Sources: TechTimes 2026-07-30, TechTimes 2026-08-03, CoreWeave IR 2026-08-10, Global Data Center Hub 2026-07-08.

dissent.view: CoreWeave successfully closed a $2.6B loan facility on August 10 2026 and a prior $2B bond was heavily oversubscribed in May 2026, suggesting lenders remain willing to extend GPU-backed credit at scale, which sits in tension with a 50% implied default probability.

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: Thirteen states with documented non-renewal waves places the indicator firmly in the 5-15 state band of the rubric; the NAIC confirms multi-regional acceleration, but improved 2024 underwriting and Citizens depopulation signal partial stabilisation, and no top-10 insurer has fully exited a major state, so the level-2 triggers are not met.
items.fact: NAIC July 31 2026 report (MCAS 2018-2024, 715 carriers) finds company-initiated non-renewal rates up 96%-216% across all four US regions; Climate Cosmos (June 2026) names 13 states with active non-renewal waves (CA, FL, TX, LA, CO, GA, OK, and others); NAIC simultaneously characterises the market as 'operationally strong overall' with improved 2024 underwriting results. Florida Citizens fell to ~385k policies by Jan 2026 (lowest since 2012), signalling partial stabilisation. No top-10 insurer confirmed fully exiting a major state in 2026. Source: NAIC CIPR report Aug 5 2026 (content.naic.org); CNBC Aug 6 2026; Climate Cosmos June 18 2026.

dissent.view: insurance.com May 2026 survey finds only 7% of homeowners experienced cancellation/non-renewal and only 2-3% cited insurer market exit as the cause, suggesting the consumer-level impact remains modest and contained

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: At least one failure (Metropolitan Capital) carries credible CRE/real-estate exposure linkage per Bisnow's court-record review, and the FDIC enforcement action preceding Community Bank & Trust's closure qualifies as a public enforcement action under the rubric — mapping squarely to ISOLATED (1). The cluster threshold (>=3 CRE-attributed failures, any >$10B, or coordinated interagency action) is not met. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: Four US bank failures in 2026 as of July 17, 2026 (FDIC failed-bank list, last updated July 17, 2026): Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust ($261M, Jan 30), Community Bank & Trust – West Georgia ($288M, May 1), Kentland Federal Savings and Loan ($3.7M, Jul 10), Small Business Bank ($73M, Jul 17). All are sub-$10B institutions. Bisnow (Feb 2, 2026) found real-estate loan exposure as a contributing factor in the Metropolitan Capital failure; FDIC issued an enforcement action against Community Bank & Trust – West Georgia in April 2026 prior to its closure (Forbes Advisor). No failure exceeded $10B in assets and no interagency emergency CRE supervisory action was identified.

dissent.view: FDIC has not publicly named CRE concentration as a formal cause for any 2026 failure; the CRE link for Metropolitan Capital is based on Bisnow's review of court records, not an official FDIC/Fed/OCC statement, which could support a CALM (0) reading if only official FDIC attributions are counted.

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: Fitch Ratings ABS index is the canonical primary source for subprime auto 60+ day delinquency; the June 2026 reading of 5.67% is the most recently reported figure and maps directly to the rubric's requested percent.
items.fact: The subprime 60-day-plus delinquency rate in June 2026 was 5.67%, down 64 basis points year-over-year, per Fitch Ratings subprime auto ABS index (Wolf Street, August 13, 2026, citing Fitch). Peak was 6.90% in January 2026.

dissent.view: 6.90% in January 2026 (all-time record high per Fitch ABS index) — some sources anchor to this figure as the 'current' level without citing subsequent months
6.80% in February 2026 per Fitch ABS index — cited by TradingEconomics as the most recent figure as of their April 2026 update

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The Milliman PPFI reports 88.7% on a market-value basis for the 100 largest plans as of end-June 2026, the most current monthly data point; this maps directly to the rubric requesting a representative large-plan funded ratio as a percent. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-06-30 data but the prior applied value was FY2026 (as of 2026-07-23) data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): funded ratio of the 100 largest U.S. public defined benefit plans slipped to 88.7% as of June 30, 2026, with plan assets of $6.116 trillion against total pension liabilities of $6.894 trillion. Source: Milliman PPFI, published July 30, 2026. https://www.milliman.com/en/insight/public-pension-funding-index-july-2026

dissent.view: Equable Institute 'State of Pensions 2026' projects the national average funded ratio at 85.0% for FY2026 across 253 statewide and municipal systems (published July 23, 2026); lower figure reflects a broader, smoothed-valuation universe.

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: One fully Board-approved new IMF arrangement (Ukraine, Feb 26 2026) falls in the trailing 6-month window; Bolivia is staff-level only and does not yet constitute an executed program under a 'talk vs. action' standard. One confirmed new program with no missed coupons maps to RISING (band 1) under the rubric.
items.fact: IMF Executive Board approved a new 48-month EFF for Ukraine (US$8.1bn) on 26 Feb 2026 (imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/02/26/pr-26066). A staff-level EFF agreement with Bolivia was reached 29 Jul 2026 (imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/07/29/pr26268) but Board approval is still pending as of the search date. No sovereign missed coupon or formal default has been identified in the Feb-Aug 2026 window; Argentina and Ecuador are in ongoing program reviews, not new arrangements.

dissent.view: If Bolivia's Board approval occurred before 2026-08-24 but was not captured in available search results, the count would rise to 2 and the rating would be CLUSTER (value=2).

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: TPR's own data confirms buffers are at or above the 250-300 bps regulatory minimum and leverage is materially reduced; no 2026 regulator flagging, margin-call episode, or forced selling event has been found in any primary source, mapping cleanly to Rubric 0 (NONE). Confidence is medium rather than high because TPR data runs only to March 2025 and no 2026-specific TPR/BoE publication was located.
items.as_of: 2025-03-31 (latest TPR data); no 2026 episode found as of 2026-08-24
items.fact: TPR Market Oversight report (data to 31 March 2025, published late 2025) states LDI market has fallen from ~£1.5tn to ~£0.7tn, rate buffers have risen to ~300 bps (vs ~150 bps pre-crisis), and daily volatility in leveraged LDI assets is 'more than 50% lower now than it was at the end of 2021'; no LDI margin crisis, forced gilt selling, or BoE/regulator intervention has been identified for 2026. Source: https://www.thepensionsregulator.gov.uk/en/document-library/research-and-analysis/market-oversight-how-well-pension-schemes-are-prepared-for-ldi-risk

dissent.view: April 2025 UK 30-yr gilt yields hit 5.6% (26-yr high), described as 'stirring memories of 2022 pension crisis' — implying latent LDI stress concern, though no forced selling or regulator action was confirmed

January 2025 gilt selloff triggered LDI cash calls at some funds (XPS, Gallagher confirmed), but all eight industry players said the response was orderly — a borderline Rubric-1 signal that resolved without escalation

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: Active BRICS non-dollar settlement agreements and official launches (BRICS Pay partial deployment, BRICS Unit gold token pilot, Argentina-China swap extension) constitute multiple new non-dollar settlement launches and official rhetoric — squarely rubric band 1. No new sovereign reserve freeze/seizure has been executed in 2026, so band 2 is not triggered.
items.fact: As of mid-2026, BRICS Pay is in partial/early operational deployment — full rollout is targeted for the New Delhi BRICS summit (Sep 2026) — and The BRICS Unit gold-backed settlement token completed a small pilot (100 units, Oct 2025). The BRICS Pay pilot launch was confirmed by Russian FM Lavrov at the 2025 Rio summit as 'targeted for end-2026' (bricspayment.ru). No new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure beyond the pre-existing frozen Russian assets (~€260bn, immobilised since 2022) has been executed; EU asset confiscation remains in deliberation, not action.

dissent.view: Some non-authoritative sources (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) claim BRICS Pay is already 'fully operational' and intra-bloc local-currency trade is 67% — overstating confirmed reality; more sober sources (EBC Financial Group, aerapass.io, bricspayment.ru) note the system remains in pilot/early-deployment phase as of mid-2026 with full rollout pending the Sep 2026 summit.

EU confiscation of ~€210bn Russian assets has been actively plotted (Art.122 mechanism, Dec 2025), but Macron, ECB, and Belgian PM have all blocked outright seizure; Brookings (Jun 2025) and CFR note all options under consideration avoid outright confiscation — so this stays as deliberation, not executed action.

items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The 2026 Trustees Report materially worsens the depletion outlook (OASI date advanced, long-run deficit up 16%), meeting rubric band 1's criterion of a trustees report worsening the depletion date. No automatic cut has been triggered nor has any legislation enacting cuts been enacted, so band 2 does not apply.
items.fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (SSA, issued 2026-06-09) projects OASI trust fund depletion in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than the prior report -- with a 75-year actuarial deficit of 4.42% of taxable payroll (up 16% from 2025). No benefit cuts have been enacted; the Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act of 2026 (H.R. 9187) and the PROMISE Act are proposed but have not been brought to a vote. Source: https://www.ssa.gov/oact/trsum/ and https://www.ssa.gov/oact/TR/2026/tr2026.pdf

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)
items.rationale: Multiple corroborating price-signal sources (Argus/Reuters, Benchmark, RareEarthExchanges, S&P Global Platts) place the heavy rare earth ex-China premium in the 4–5x range for the primary magnet HREEs (dysprosium, terbium) as of mid-to-late 2026, anchored by actual transaction data and export volume declines (~50% shipping drop per Chinese customs); best single estimate is ~4.5x as the central tendency across sources, consistent with the volume signal confirming genuine supply bifurcation rather than a paper premium.
items.fact: As of August 17, 2026, Rare Earth Exchanges reports terbium assessed at $3,600–$5,000+/kg in Western markets vs ~$989–998/kg China domestic (implying ~3.6x–5.0x), while Argus data cited by Reuters (Oregon Group, June 2026) puts dysprosium and terbium oxide ex-China prices at 4x–5x Chinese domestic references; Benchmark Minerals (March 2026) pegged 2025 dysprosium CIF North America at 4.4x EXW China.

Serra Verde–USA Rare Earth contractual floors ($575/kg Dy, $2,050/kg Tb) imply only ~2x Chinese reference prices, but these are long-term contracted floors, not spot market levels

items.label: Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
items.rationale: Both sides have enacted new measures within the trailing 3-month window: the US through the MATCH Act legislative push and VEU revocations (tightening), and China through counter-jurisdiction regulations and expanded rare-earth export licensing (retaliation with a corroborating commodity price spike). Rubric level 2 (RETALIATION) is met: the target country has enacted active countermeasures including legal retaliation tools and input-supply controls.
items.fact: US side: MATCH Act (introduced April 2, 2026) proposes blanket DUV lithography ban to China; VEU exemptions for Samsung/SK Hynix/TSMC/Micron revoked; Commerce Dept pressing ASML on EUV diversion since April 2026 (Reuters/CNBC, July 2026). dissent.view: East Asia Forum (March 2026) characterises the White House as having 'cooled' chip export controls and suspending further restrictions under Trump trade-talk priorities, suggesting the executive branch has partially softened enforcement even as Congress escalates -- this would cap the read closer to 1 if only executive action counts.

items.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
items.rationale: Hormuz traffic is severely suppressed (~7% of pre-crisis daily rate) with active attacks and a blockade — well under 25% — but U.S. naval-escorted convoys continue moving non-Iranian cargo and Brent at ~$95 is elevated but not at the April closure-panic peak of $121, which the rubric requires to confirm a '2'. Both corridors are therefore CONTESTED (1): physically threatened, partially disrupted, moving under naval escort, with no functioning ceasefire or MoU in force.
items.fact: Lloyd's List Intelligence (Aug 19, 2026): 73 transits through Strait of Hormuz in week of Aug 10-16 vs ~138/day pre-conflict; the June 17 MoU expired Aug 17 without agreement, Iran resumed attacks on commercial vessels, U.S. blockade of Iranian ports active, yet non-Iranian traffic continues in both directions under U.S. naval escort. dissent.view: straits.live (Aug 23, 2026) characterises the Strait as 'effectively closed to commercial shipping' citing 1 transit on Aug 16 vs ~73/day normal — a rating-2 framing; however this conflicts with Lloyd's List JMIC data showing 73 transits in the full week of Aug 10-16 and U.S. military convoy operations, so rubric caps at 1.

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)
items.rationale: Six distinct new trade measures across three major economies in the trailing 3 months exceeds the rubric threshold of >=4 for ESCALATING; the USTR 12.5% action alone also qualifies as a broad tariff round (>=10% across a sector -- here all Chinese goods), satisfying two independent ESCALATING triggers.
items.fact: At least 6 new major-economy trade measures against China (or by China) in trailing 3 months: (1) USTR new 12.5% Section 301 tariff on ALL Chinese goods effective 24 Jul 2026 (China-Briefing, 23 Jul 2026 update; https://www.china-briefing.com/news/us-china-tariff-rates-2025/); (2) EU definitive anti-dumping duty on Chinese polyamide yarns (Regulation EU 2026/1823, 28 Jul 2026; cambioslegales.es); (3) China MOFCOM provisional anti-dumping deposits up to 54.3% on US/Mexican pecans, effective 11 Aug 2026 (Global Times/MOFCOM); (4) China MOFCOM+MOF export control and procurement bans on 56 US entities, 22 Jun 2026 (Arnold & Porter); (5) China export bans on 14 EU defense/tech/chemical companies, ~3 Aug 2026 (Mondaq/Steptoe); (6) China MOFCOM national security investigation into imported printing/copying equipment, 5 Aug 2026 (MOFCOM Announcement No. 33 of 2026).

items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: Two rubric triggers for Score 1 are both met: (a) <90 days to the Nov 10 2026 nominal expiry with no extension announced, and (b) a partial breach via new entity-list additions on June 22 2026. dissent.view: FDD (2026-06-24) characterises the June 22 entity-list actions as ending 'the pause', implying Score 2; however this is contradicted by the blanket suspension remaining formally in place and Reuters/Benchmark analysts calling the measures narrow and symbolic.

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The regime is case-by-case for most shippers (general licences confined to a narrow whitelist), processing times structurally exceed 30 days (60-120 days in practice), and new categories were added to the control list within the trailing 3 months — all squarely within rubric level 1 (SLOWING). No announced categorical denial or licensing suspension exists to justify level 2. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: The April 2025 rare-earth magnet licensing regime (covering dysprosium, terbium and magnets containing them) is fully in force and was never suspended. MOFCOM's statutory target is 45 working days (~9 weeks), but industry reporting (GetTransport/Duramag, July 2026) shows heavy-REE magnet approvals routinely run 60-120+ days. General licences exist but are limited to a small whitelist of pre-cleared Chinese exporters (first batch: JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng, Dec 2025); the scheme 'is not broadly available yet.' In June 2026 China added 10 US firms to its export control list (Morgan Lewis, July 1 2026), and Trump threatened 200% tariffs in August 2026 over continued supply delays (China Briefing, Aug 2026). The 2026 licensing catalogue added samarium, gadolinium and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories (Certivo, Mar 2026). No categorical denial or suspension of licensing has been announced.

dissent.view: MERICS (undated 2025/2026) notes a MOFCOM 'green channel' and EU whitelist have allowed magnet exports to the EU to pick up since May 2025, suggesting some easing for civilian buyers; this could be read as partial normalisation toward level 0 for EU-bound civilian flows.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Persistent daily median-line crossings and regular naval presence constitute assertive patrols above routine, meeting rubric level 1 (ELEVATED); the Jul 24-25 live-fire drill reinforces this. No blockade, kinetic engagement, or full mobilization evidence exists to justify level 2.

items.label: Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

items.label: China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)

dissent.view: Fertilizer Daily (Jul 29 2026) reports China 'extended' phosphate curbs through August 2026, which could be interpreted as a new tightening action if the extension was formally enacted post-May 24 — but the underlying suspension was set in Dec 2025 and the extension appears to be a continuation, not a new restriction on additional products.

items.label: Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)

Jurisdictions with enacted pauses/moratoria include: New York (statewide EO), Maine (passed legislature, vetoed), South Dakota (local-enabling law SB 135), Georgia (multiple counties), Virginia (Prince William County invalidation), Texas Hill County (briefly enacted then rescinded), plus 100+ other local jurisdictions per DLA Piper.

Kathy Hochul signed an Executive Order on July 14, 2026, creating the nation's first statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, pausing state environmental permits for up to one year for facilities at 50 MW or more (Axios / NY Governor press release, 2026-07-14). Maine's legislature passed a statewide moratorium (later vetoed). South Dakota passed SB 135 enabling local bans. Multiple counties in Georgia, Virginia (Prince William County), and Texas (Hill County) enacted local pauses.

WilmerHale (Aug 2026) states 'legislators in six states have introduced ten similar bills' at the state level, a lower count than DLA Piper's '12 states,' reflecting different cutoff dates and counting methodologies.

items.rationale: Four or more top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, Caserones, Codelco Andina/El Teniente, Antofagasta Los Pelambres) carry confirmed active production cuts as of the rating date, well exceeding the >=3 threshold; multiple institutions (Benchmark, Goldman Sachs) have explicitly forecast a refined copper market deficit as a result, satisfying both prongs of the CLUSTER criterion.

As of the SEC commissioner August 2026 update (sec.gov, ~Aug 7 2026), those dates remain unchanged and no second extension has been announced; however, SIFMA and IIB exemptive-relief requests are actively pending before the Commission (published Apr 17 2026), comment periods on combined inter-affiliate/extraterritorial relief and a 15c3-3 net-omnibus margin exemption closed Aug 31 2026, and the SEC has granted conditional exemptive relief for captive clearing subsidiaries for private funds - all consistent with multiple open exemptive-relief requests still pending.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The 10-year JGB yield has risen well over 50 bps from its early-2026 baseline on fiscal concerns, but auctions continue to clear (5y BTC 4.15, no failed auction cited) and no BOJ emergency operation has been triggered; the FY2027 fiscal/funding path remains unspecified. This pattern — large yield move on fiscal news, auctions still clearing, no disorderly failure — maps squarely to rubric level 1 (UNCLEAR: funding path unspecified OR >25 bps yield move on fiscal news but auctions still clearing).
items.fact: The 10-year JGB yield closed at ~2.88% on 21 Aug 2026 and intra-week touched 2.95% — levels last seen in 1996 — driven by fiscal uncertainty around the Takaichi administration's FY2027 budget planning and continued supplementary-budget debt concerns. That represents a rise of roughly +60-70 bps from the ~2.1-2.2% range seen in Feb-Mar 2026, and +87 bps from the ~2.0% level when Takaichi first took office. The most recent JGB auction data shows the 5-year sale on 18 Aug 2026 cleared with a bid-to-cover of 4.15 (strong), while the MOF 20-year auction on 20 Aug 2026 cleared without a reported failure. No BOJ emergency operation has been cited. Funding path for the upcoming FY2027 budget remains unspecified amid markets 'bracing for next phase of fiscal planning' (Nikkei Asia, 19 Aug 2026). Oxford Economics noted the 10y yield 'risen sharply from 2.1% in March, fuelled by market concern about Japan's more aggressive fiscal stance' (Oxford Economics, Jun 2026). Sources: TradingEconomics (22 Aug 2026), Nikkei Asia (19 Aug 2026), Bloomberg (18 Aug 2026), Oxford Economics (Jun 2026).

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~78–100%+ YoY) materially exceeds AI-revenue growth in growth-rate terms, satisfying the WIDE condition; however, AI-attributable cloud revenue is accelerating QoQ across all four hyperscalers and no company cut its AI-revenue outlook — ruling out the WIDENING FAST (2) classification which requires deceleration or an outlook cut.
items.fact: Q2 2026 earnings: combined hyperscaler 2026 capex guidance raised to ~$730B (~+78% YoY vs ~$410B in 2025); Alphabet Q2 capex $44.9B (~+~100% YoY), Microsoft FY26 cash capex +80% YoY, Meta Q2 capex $31.08B (+83% YoY), Amazon 2026 capex raised to ~$220B. Meanwhile AI-attributable cloud revenue accelerated QoQ: Google Cloud +82% YoY in Q2 (vs +63% Q1), AWS +37% YoY (vs +28% Q1), Azure +43% YoY (vs +40% Q1); AWS AI business annualized >$25B 'more than doubling YoY' (CNBC/Amazon Q2 2026 earnings, July 30 2026; Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings release, SEC, July 22 2026). UBS estimates hyperscalers will spend ~102% of cloud revenue on capex in 2026 (Yahoo Finance, Aug 2026).

items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: YTD insured losses of $42-47bn are materially BELOW the 10-year average (not above it, let alone >150%), and the largest single H1 2026 event was ~$5bn (U.S. SCS late-April outbreak) -- well under the $10bn threshold. Both the ELEVATED and SEVERE thresholds are unmet, mapping cleanly to NORMAL (0).
items.fact: H1 2026 global insured natural catastrophe losses: Swiss Re Institute estimates $42bn (16% below 10-year trend of ~$66bn); Gallagher Re estimates $46bn (28% below 10-year average of $64bn); Aon estimates $47bn. No single event exceeded $10bn insured -- five consecutive quarters without a >$10bn event. Sources: Swiss Re Institute (swissre.com, ~Aug 20 2026), Gallagher Re H1 2026 NatCat Report (ajg.com/gallagherre, Jul 15 2026), Aon H1 2026 Global Cat Recap (artemis.bm, Jul 22 2026).

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: The government is a self-described 'fragile minority' coalition in a hung parliament, surviving via Socialist abstentions and Article 49.3 — the textbook definition of rubric band 1. No confidence vote has been lost, no PM resignation since Oct 6 2025 (resolved by re-appointment), and no snap election has been called, ruling out band 2.
items.fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's second minority government (formed 10 Oct 2025) remains incumbent. It survived four no-confidence votes (Oct 16 2025, Jan 14 2026, Feb 2 2026 x2), invoked Article 49.3 on Jan 20 2026 to force the 2026 budget, and the budget passed Feb 2 2026. Sources: France 24 (20 Jan 2026), Al Jazeera (2 Feb 2026), Euronews (23 Jan 2026), Wikipedia Lecornu governments.

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)
items.rationale: Two of the three major agencies (Fitch on 12 Sep 2025, S&P on ~17 Oct 2025) executed actual one-notch rating cuts from AA- to A+ within the trailing 12 months; rubric 2 requires only one actual cut in the trailing 12 months, which is clearly satisfied. Moody's negative-outlook action is subsumed by the higher severity of the executed downgrades.
items.fact: S&P Global Ratings downgraded France from 'AA-' to 'A+' (stable outlook) on ~17 October 2025 (spglobal.com article dated Oct 17 2025: 'France Ratings Lowered To A+/A-1 From AA-/A-1+'). Fitch had already downgraded France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) on 12 September 2025 (France24, CNBC, ING Think, Sep 13-15 2025). Moody's on 25 October 2025 kept Aa3 but moved outlook to negative (France24, Oct 25 2025).

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: The signed figure is +3.5% YoY for July 2026, released by NBS on 2026-08-10; rubric scores on SIZE of move — at +3.5% this represents a notable cost-push signal that has reversed a prolonged deflation streak, flagging potential input-cost pressure spillover to trading partners.
items.fact: NBS official press release (stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202608/t20260810_1965017.html, released 2026-08-10): 'In July 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 3.5% year on year and decreased by 0.7% month on month.' Corroborated by Xinhua (2026-08-09) and China Daily (2026-08-09).

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Both MP Materials and USA Rare Earth are explicitly named on MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (22 June 2026), satisfying rubric level 1 (entity-specific listing of named US producers). All authoritative sources, including Benchmark Minerals and Arnold & Porter, characterise the measure as entity-specific rather than a blanket or sector-wide restriction, ruling out level 2.
items.fact: China MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to its export-control list under the Export Control Law and Dual-Use Items Regulations, explicitly including MP Materials Corp and USA Rare Earth. The restriction is firm-specific: Chinese companies and individuals are barred from supplying dual-use goods to these named entities. Multiple corroborating sources (Benchmark Minerals, Arnold & Porter, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, ORF, The Oregon Group) confirm the listing date and named firms. Market reaction was muted -- MP Materials was roughly flat and USA Rare Earth modestly higher on the announcement day -- consistent with a targeted, entity-level action rather than a sector-wide shock.

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: The composite FFPI is rising both MoM (+0.6%) and YoY (+1.0%), placing it in the ELEVATED band; the MoM gain is well below the 3% upper boundary for band 1 and far below the 5% SPIKING threshold, even though sub-components (wheat +5.8%, sugar +6%) individually spiked.
items.fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.6% MoM from June 2026 (130.3) and 1.0% above July 2025; highest reading since January 2023. Source: FAO official press release, fao.org/newsroom, released 2026-08-07.

items.label: Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
items.rationale: Storage at ~26.6-27% of capacity is below the 30% CRITICAL threshold, independently satisfying rubric criterion 1. Elevation of ~1,039-1,041 ft is also ~9-11 ft below Hoover Dam minimum power pool (~1,050 ft), satisfying the 'within 15 feet of a power-generation threshold' criterion; both sub-criteria for rating 2 are met with confirmed physical data.
items.fact: Lake Mead elevation 1,039.44 ft, storage 26.6% of capacity as of Aug 20 2026 (reservoirbench.com citing USBR daily gauge); USBR Lower Colorado Weekly Update (Aug 3 2026) corroborates at 1,040.96 ft / 27% of capacity. Hoover Dam minimum power pool is ~1,050 ft, placing Mead ~10-11 ft below that threshold.

flags.name: Two Hormuz reads disagree on the same strait
flags.message: Gulf fertilizer inputs are rated CUT (2, i.e. closure) but the sea-lane indicator rates the very same Strait of Hormuz only CONTESTED (<=1). They track one physical chokepoint and must agree - align the fertilizer read down to DISRUPTED (1) unless the strait is genuinely closed.

flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
